title: Steve Jobs at Aspen 1983: why computers must be designed beautifully, and the case for great people
summary: At the 1983 International Design Conference in Aspen, Jobs frames the personal computer as a new medium, pleads with designers to make it beautiful instead of another piece of junk, and explains Apple's push to put a great computer in a book. He also describes hiring exceptional people, keeping teams small and flat, and bringing the liberal arts into technology.

principles.text: Computers will sell regardless, so make them great: beauty costs no more.
principles.quote: it doesn't cost any more money to make it look great

principles.text: A new object entering everyone's life is a chance to put a great object there or one more piece of junk.
principles.quote: we have a shot at putting a great object there or if we don't we're going to put one more piece of junk object there

principles.text: Hire people far better than the current job needs; they will be stretching within months.
principles.quote: we've always tried to hire people that were much better than we needed for the current job because within six months they'd be fighting to keep up with it

principles.text: A few exceptional people outperform many good ones, so keep the team small.
principles.quote: we think there are people that are so good that they can run circles around five pretty good people okay and those are the kind of people that we want at Apple

principles.text: Hire people to tell you what to do, and give them an environment where they don't have to convince dozens of others.
principles.quote: the reason we hire people is to tell us what to do

principles.text: Technology must be infused with the liberal arts: better type, fonts and graphics so people deal in pictures, not just text.
principles.quote: we're solving the problems of injecting some liberal arts into these computers
